subject: geography
topicDisplay: Trade In The Contemporary World Global Migration Human Rights Power Borders
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: The North American Free Trade Agreement (now USMCA) is an example of a:
questions.explain: NAFTA/USMCA is a regional trade agreement reducing barriers between the USA, Canada and Mexico.

questions.q: A major criticism of Rostow's model is that it:
options: Is Eurocentric and assumes all countries follow the same Western path
questions.explain: Critics argue the model wrongly universalises the Western experience and ignores colonial and global structural barriers.

questions.q: Why can a country have a high GNI per capita but a low HDI?
options: Wealth may be unevenly invested, leaving health and education indicators weak
questions.explain: Resource-rich states can have high average income yet poor schooling and life expectancy if wealth is not invested in people.

questions.q: Which term best describes the increasing interconnectedness and interdependence of the world's economies, cultures and populations?
questions.explain: Globalisation is the process by which the world's economies, societies and cultures become increasingly integrated and interdependent.

questions.q: Which technology has been the single most important enabler of the globalisation of services and finance since the 1990s?
questions.explain: ICT, including the internet and fibre-optics, allows instant global communication and 24-hour trading.

questions.q: A global production network in which a TNC sources components from many countries illustrates the concept of:
questions.explain: A spatial division of labour spreads different stages of production across locations with cost or skill advantages.

questions.q: The Social Progress Index is notable because it deliberately excludes which variable?
questions.explain: The Social Progress Index measures social and environmental outcomes without using economic indicators, complementing GDP.

questions.q: Which institution lends to countries facing short-term balance-of-payments crises, often attaching austerity conditions?
questions.explain: The International Monetary Fund (IMF) provides emergency lending, frequently with structural adjustment conditions.

questions.q: A 'race to the bottom' in globalisation most directly refers to countries competing by:
options: Lowering wages, taxes and regulations to attract TNCs
questions.explain: The 'race to the bottom' describes states cutting standards and costs to attract footloose investment.

questions.q: Demographic globalisation is most clearly illustrated by:
options: The spread of the US dollar
The international migration of people for work
questions.explain: Demographic globalisation involves international migration and the changing distribution of population.

questions.q: Remittances are best defined as:
options: Money sent home by international migrant workers
questions.explain: Remittances are funds transferred by migrants to their home country, an important flow for many economies.

questions.q: Why is gender equality considered central to development?
options: It only matters in high-income countries
Empowering women raises education, health, productivity and reduces poverty
questions.explain: Educating and empowering women improves household welfare, child outcomes and economic growth, accelerating development.

questions.q: Which UN measure underpins the international framework for human rights?
options: The Universal Declaration of Human Rights (1948)
questions.explain: The 1948 Universal Declaration of Human Rights sets out the foundational global standard for human rights.

questions.q: When a global brand adapts its products to suit local tastes and customs, this is known as:
questions.explain: Glocalisation is the adaptation of global products and services to local markets and cultures.

questions.q: What is meant by the 'development gap'?
options: The time lag before a census is published
A shortfall in a government's annual budget
The widening difference in living standards between the richest and poorest
The difference between GDP and GNI
questions.explain: The development gap describes the disparity in wealth and quality of life between the most and least developed nations.

questions.q: Which is an example of global political governance attempting to manage shared problems?
options: The United Nations and international climate agreements
questions.explain: Bodies like the UN and agreements such as the Paris accord represent global governance of shared issues.

questions.q: Why is GNI per capita (PPP) often preferred to GDP for comparing living standards between countries?
options: It adjusts for differences in the cost of living and includes income from abroad
It excludes the informal economy entirely
questions.explain: GNI counts income earned abroad, and PPP adjustment corrects for differing price levels so values are more comparable.

questions.q: What three dimensions does the Human Development Index (HDI) combine?
questions.explain: The HDI is a composite of GNI per capita (income), schooling (education) and life expectancy (health).

questions.q: The 'global shift' of manufacturing to Asia has, for many older industrial regions in the Global North, caused:
questions.explain: Loss of manufacturing to lower-cost economies has driven deindustrialisation in regions like the UK's north.

questions.q: The interdependence created by globalisation means that:
options: An economic shock in one country can rapidly spread to others
questions.explain: Interdependence means events such as the 2008 financial crisis transmit quickly through linked economies.

questions.q: Which of these is primarily a dimension of ECONOMIC globalisation?
options: The diffusion of the English language
The spread of fast-food culture worldwide
The growth of global financial flows and trade
questions.explain: Economic globalisation refers to the growing scale of trade, investment and financial flows across borders.

questions.q: The dominance of Western (often American) culture worldwide is sometimes criticised as:
questions.explain: Cultural homogenisation, or 'McDonaldisation', describes the erosion of local diversity by dominant global culture.

questions.q: The 'trade vs aid' debate centres on whether development is better promoted by:
options: Long-term self-sustaining trade or short-term external aid
questions.explain: The debate weighs the long-term independence of trade-led growth against the dependency risks of aid.

questions.q: The standardisation of shipping containers from the 1950s is a key example of which driver of globalisation?
questions.explain: Containerisation dramatically cut the cost and time of moving goods, accelerating global trade.

questions.q: Special Economic Zones (SEZs), such as those pioneered in China, attract investment mainly by offering:
options: Tax incentives, relaxed regulation and cheap labour
questions.explain: SEZs use tax breaks, deregulation and low-cost labour to draw export-oriented foreign investment.

questions.q: Fairtrade schemes aim to address inequalities in globalisation primarily by:
options: Removing all tariffs on luxury goods
Guaranteeing producers a minimum price and a social premium
questions.explain: Fairtrade guarantees minimum prices and a premium to give producers in poorer countries a fairer return.

questions.q: What is the epidemiological (health) transition?
options: A change from manual to automated farming
A move from rural to urban living
A shift from communicable to non-communicable diseases as a country develops
The spread of a single pandemic globally
questions.explain: As development raises life expectancy, the main disease burden shifts from infectious to chronic, lifestyle-related conditions.

questions.q: Reducing tariffs, quotas and other barriers to international trade is known as:
questions.explain: Trade liberalisation removes barriers to trade and has been a major driver of globalisation.

questions.q: In Rostow's model, the 'take-off' stage is characterised by what?
options: Rapid industrialisation and rising investment in key sectors
questions.explain: Take-off involves a surge in manufacturing and investment that drives sustained, self-reinforcing growth.

questions.q: Which statement about the winners and losers of globalisation is most accurate?
options: Globalisation has had no effect on inequality
Benefits and costs are unevenly distributed within and between countries
questions.explain: Globalisation creates uneven outcomes, with some groups and regions gaining and others losing.
